Issued at 316 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

Today will be partly cloudy and breezy. Southerly winds increase 
through the morning as an upper shortwave and surface low pressure 
move in from the west. Areas along and west of I-29 can expect gusts 
of 20-30 mph with the strongest gusts over south central South 
Dakota. Here occasional gusts to 35 mph are possible. Areas to 
the east of I-29 will see gusts of 20 mph or less. Winds will 
bring in warmer temperatures and moisture, boosting dew points 
into the mid to upper 60s F. With highs expected to climb into 
the 80s and low 90s today will feel bit muggy. 

This afternoon and through the overnight SPC has issued a Day 1 
Marginal (level 1 of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorms that covers 
most of the CWA. A marginal to slightly unstable environment will 
develop through today with 1500-2500 J/kg of MUCAPE, 35-45 kts of 
deep layer shear, and steep mid-level lapse rates. However, 
uncertainty in storm development is high due to a couple of factors. 
First is cloud cover, should morning clouds linger through the day 
it may limit surface heating, therefore limiting instability. 
Guidance has some variation on the timing of the wave and 
amplification of the LLJ. The GFS and EC continue to have the wave 
and LLJ move through earlier, while the CAN and NAM are slower. 
Similarly, CAMs guidance is split with the HRRR, NamNest, and RAP13 
showing earlier initiation while the ARW and FV3 are later. With the 
earlier solutions it is more likely that initial convection will 
begin as super cells that grow upscale into a line, possibly with 
bowing segments. The slower solutions will more likely begin as 
elevated multicell convection that grows into a line with bowing 
segments. As of 2:30 pm CDT a cumulus field is forming over western 
and central South Dakota, some producing light radar echoes. This 
could be an indication that the cap is weakening, thus an indication 
that earlier convective initiation may be the correct solution. That 
being said, the greatest severe risk still looks to be between 10 pm 
tonight through 6 am Saturday. Hazards are heavy rain, 1.5 to 2 inch 
hail (with supercells west of the James River Valley), and wind 
gusts 60-65 mph. As storm progress east they will become elevated 
and transition to more of a wind and heavy rain threat. Greatest 
risk area is along and north of I-90. 

A few showers and storms may linger into mid-Saturday morning before 
pushing east of the CWA. Through the day the surface low associated 
with the previous storms will drift east, pushing clouds out of the 
region. Southerly winds will remain breezy gusting up to 30 mph. 
Warm and moist air continues to advect into the region. Highs will 
climb into the upper 80s to mid 90s, and dew points to the mid 60s 
to low 70s. Heat Index values will climb into the 90s, with areas 
along the southern Missouri River Valley potentially reaching 100. 
At this time a Heat Advisory is not necessary, however we will 
monitor the trends. Storm chances return for late Saturday evening 
into Sunday morning. Looking aloft a deepening upper trough will 
push east into the north central Rockies. On the east side of the 
mountains a subtle mid-level lee trough and surface low form. As 
this begins to drift east late in the afternoon along with an area 
of enhanced vorticity it could trigger showers and thunderstorms. A 
marginally unstable environment with steep mid-level lapse rates and 
35 kts of deep layer shear may support isolated to scattered strong 
to severe thunderstorms, mainly over central South Dakota. SPC has 
issued a Day 2 Marginal Risk west of a line from roughly Huron, to 
Plankinton, to Bonesteel. For this area hazards include large 
hail and damaging wind gusts. As storms drift east they will 
encounter a less favorable environment and should weaken. 
Similar to Friday- Saturday, confidence in storm formation is 
low due to the conditional nature of cloud clearing, a strongly 
capped environment, and variance in guidance on storm track and
timing. 

Sunday brings yet a third round of potentially strong to severe 
thunderstorms. SPC has issued a Day 3 Marginal that encompasses 
the entire CWA. A marginally unstable environment is expected 
for the afternoon and evening. Stronger forcing this round as an
upper closed low skirting the international border drags a cold
front through the northern Plains Sunday evening into Monday 
morning. Mid- range guidance is in very low agreement on track 
and timing of this system. In addition, south to southwest winds
for western and central South Dakota advect in a drier air mass
than the previous two days. This general lack of moisture will 
likely prevent convection from forming over this region. At the 
same time over eastern South Dakota and Nebraska, and western 
Minnesota and Iowa moisture rich air will pool south of the warm
front. As the cold front approaches this area showers and 
thunderstorms may form. Coverage of storms
